title: Migration: why people move, and what it does

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: What migration is, the push and pull factors behind it, and the impacts it has on the place left, the place joined and the migrants themselves.

blocks.heading: What migration is
blocks.text: Migration is a move to live somewhere else, not a visit or a seasonal stay for work alone. Internal migration stays within one country, and the largest internal stream in most countries is the move from countryside to city. International migration crosses a national border, which is what makes it need papers, permission or risk. Wherever the move ends, it has a place of origin and a destination, and every reason for it belongs to one side or the other.

blocks.heading: Push and pull
blocks.text: Push factors are things about the origin that make people want to leave: a poor harvest, no work, low pay, few schools and clinics, or danger. Pull factors are things about the destination that attract: better-paid jobs, services, family already settled, safer and more stable conditions. A migration usually needs both, because a reason to leave does not by itself say where to go, and an attraction does not by itself force anyone out of the origin. Migration streams then follow routes people can afford and are allowed to use: distance, cost, borders and information filter who moves, so most international migrants from a poor region head for the nearest country with work, or for one where relatives have already settled and can pass on jobs, rooms and know-how.

blocks.heading: Whose side is the question on?
blocks.text: Migration has separate impacts on the origin, the destination and the migrants, and the commonest error is answering for the wrong one: writing about the migrants when the question asks about the destination, or listing problems when it asks for benefits. Before writing, decide whose side the question asks about, and keep every sentence on that side.

blocks.heading: Impacts on the origin
blocks.text: A village that loses its young adults to the city or abroad feels the loss and the gain together. The departure leaves fewer workers to farm the land and fewer carers for the old, so some fields go unploughed and grandparents raise children alone. But the migrants send money home, and those remittances build houses, pay school fees and lift the families left above what local work could pay.

blocks.heading: Impacts on the destination
blocks.text: A city or country that receives many migrants gains workers who fill jobs, often the work local people avoid, and pay taxes into services as their children enter the schools. But rapid arrivals strain housing and services before they can grow, rents can rise, and resentment can build where the newcomers are blamed for crowding. Some migrants end up in poor-quality, overcrowded housing because that is all the market offers them on arrival.

blocks.heading: Impacts on the migrants
blocks.text: For the movers themselves, the balance usually improves: pay is higher, children enter better schools, and the move can lift a whole family's prospects. The costs are real too: families are separated across borders, language and paperwork slow people down, and undocumented or unskilled arrivals are open to exploitation because complaining risks the job or the stay.

blocks.text: The reasons populations grow and shrink are topic 1.1; net migration, immigrants minus emigrants, is one of the two causes of population change named there.
